title: What a Struct Looks Like in Memory: Where Each Member Goes, and the Order That Wastes Least

questions.question: A struct holds a uint64_t and a uint8_t, nine bytes of members. What is its sizeof?
options: 16: the struct is padded at the end to a multiple of its own alignment, so that the second element of an array keeps its uint64_t aligned
It depends on the order
questions.explanation: The size of a struct is never the sum of the sizes of its members.

questions.question: A byte, a double and a byte are 24 bytes as written. What is the size with the double first?
options: 16: the bytes follow the double at 8 and 9, and the end is padded to 16
24, the order does not matter
questions.explanation: Written the other way the double skips to 8, the second byte to 16, and the end is padded to 24.

questions.question: How does align_up round an offset to a multiple of the alignment?
options: It masks the low bits of an odd number
It adds the alignment
It uses a floating point round
It adds alignment minus one and divides and multiplies back, where integer division throws the remainder away

questions.question: The lesson tried every order of 400 random structs. What did that show about putting the most strictly aligned member first?
options: It gave the smallest size in all 400, so for alignments that are powers of two it is the best order there is
It made no difference
It was often best
It was sometimes worse
questions.explanation: It saved up to 32 bytes against the order written.

questions.question: A record held 29 bytes of data in 48 bytes of struct as written and 32 in the best order. What is the effect on a million of them?
options: None
48 MB against 32 MB, and a 64 byte cache line holds 1.3 records against 2.0
16 MB less, with no effect on speed
The same, because data is the same
questions.explanation: Padding is not free: it is memory and it is cache, and it is paid for on every read.

questions.question: What does a static_assert on sizeof of a record protect against?
options: Nothing
A field added later, or one whose alignment changed, quietly growing the record: it becomes a compile error and not a surprise in a log file
A slower build
Wrong data in the fields
questions.explanation: Sixteen bytes can be lost to one member in the wrong place and nothing else fails.
